From LLMs to LRMs: Rethinking Pruning for Reasoning-Centric Models

Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly costly to deploy, motivating extensive research on model pruning. However, most existing studies focus on instruction-following LLMs, leaving it unclear whether established pruning strategies transfer to reasoning-augmented models that explicitly generate long intermediate reasoning traces. In this work, we conduct a controlled study of pruning for both instruction-following (LLM-instruct) and reasoning-augmented (LLM-think) models. To isolate the effects of pruning, we align pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery data with each model’s original training distribution, which we show yield more stable and reliable pruning behavior. We evaluate static depth pruning, static width pruning, and dynamic pruning across 17 tasks spanning classification, generation, and reasoning. Our results reveal clear paradigm-dependent differences: depth pruning outperforms width pruning on classification tasks, while width pruning is more robust for generation and reasoning. Moreover, static pruning better preserves reasoning performance, whereas dynamic pruning excels on classification and generation but remains challenging for long-chain reasoning. These findings underscore the need for pruning strategies that explicitly account for the distinct characteristics of reasoning-augmented LLMs. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LRM-Pruning.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have led to significant advances in natural language processing and enabled impactful applications across a wide range of domains Zhu et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2024); Pang et al. (2024); Abbasian et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2024); Guan et al. (2025). However, their strong empirical performance comes with substantial computational costs, posing major challenges for practical use in resource-constrained environments (Zhong et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025).

Model pruning has emerged as one of the most widely adopted approaches for improving LLM efficiency Sun et al. (2024); Ma et al. (2023); Men et al. (2024). Early work has primarily focused on static pruning, where a fixed subset of parameters is removed prior to deployment. Within this paradigm, static depth pruning reduces inference cost by removing entire layers, shortening the model and decreasing sequential computation (Men et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024). In contrast, static width pruning reduces per-layer computation by shrinking hidden dimensions or pruning channels while preserving the original network depth (Ma et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024). More recently, dynamic pruning has been explored, which adaptively skips parts of the computation during inference based on input-dependent signals, rather than permanently removing parameters (Raposo et al., 2024a; Jiang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). Together, these techniques form a mature toolkit for accelerating LLMs.

Meanwhile, the LLM landscape is undergoing a paradigm shift from instruction-following models, which we refer to as LLM-instruct, to reasoning-augmented models, denoted as LLM-think Xu et al. (2025); DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025). Unlike LLM-instruct (Yang et al., 2024a), which generate a direct response with reasoning implicitly embedded, LLM-think explicitly externalize their reasoning process by producing step-by-step intermediate traces prior to the final answer (Wei et al., 2022). While this shift substantially improves performance on complex tasks, it also results in markedly longer generations, often spanning thousands of tokens (Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a). Despite these fundamental changes in model behavior and output characteristics, existing pruning research has almost exclusively focused on LLM-instruct. This gap motivates a central question: does pruning for LLM-think require new strategies, or can existing approaches generalize across paradigms?

Addressing this question necessitates a carefully controlled pruning pipeline. We therefore begin by revisiting a critical yet often overlooked design choice in prior work: the selection of datasets used for pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery. However, prior studies adopt highly heterogeneous datasets for these stages, ranging from general-domain corpora to instruction-tuning data, often without systematic justification (Raffel et al., 2020; Taori et al., 2023). Such inconsistency introduces confounding factors, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of pruning from those of distribution mismatch.

To enable a principled comparison, we adopt a controlled setting in which calibration and recovery data are strictly aligned with the original training distribution of the target model. Under this setting, we construct matched model–dataset pairs for both paradigms. For LLM-instruct, we use the open-sourced Tulu model (Lambert et al., 2024) together with its full instruction-following fine-tuning corpus. For LLM-think, we derive a reasoning-augmented counterpart by further fine-tuning the same base model on OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2025), a dataset designed to elicit explicit multi-step reasoning across diverse difficulty levels. This alignment ensures that each model is pruned, calibrated, and recovered using data drawn from its own training distribution, thereby isolating the impact of pruning itself. As we show empirically, such alignment best preserves pre-pruning performance and leads to substantially more stable and effective pruning behavior compared to using mismatched datasets.

Under this controlled setting, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three categories of pruning strategies on both LLM-instruct and LLM-think across 17 diverse classification, generation, and reasoning tasks. Our experiments yield several key empirical findings. First, static depth pruning is more effective than static width pruning on classification tasks, whereas the opposite trend holds for generation and reasoning tasks, where width pruning degrades performance more gracefully. Second, dynamic pruning with unconstrained token-level routing benefits classification and generation but proves substantially harder to optimize for long-chain reasoning, suggesting that aggressive computation skipping is particularly risky for reasoning-intensive workloads. Finally, while dynamic pruning generally outperforms static methods on classification and generation, static pruning retains higher performance on reasoning tasks, highlighting an important gap in current dynamic pruning approaches.

2 Background

LLM-instruct and LLM-thinking

The rapid progress of LLMs has not only improved their instruction-following ability but also expanded their scope toward explicit reasoning. This shift has given rise to two major families: instruction-following models (LLM-instruct), which are optimized to produce outputs that closely align with user-specified instructions, and reasoning-augmented models (LLM-think), which are trained to generate long chains of thought (CoT) reasoning before arriving at final answers. Although the two are built upon the same underlying architecture, recent studies show that they diverge significantly in both internal representations and emergent behaviors. Mechanistically, LLM-think retain richer contextual information across layers and exhibit higher token-level entropy (Skean et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). In terms of attention, LLM-instruct generally display diverse specialization across heads, with each attending to different token subsets (Fu et al., 2024), whereas LLM-think show considerable overlap in tokens attended by different heads (Yang et al., 2025b).

Formalizing Structure Pruning Strategies

Model pruning in LLMs can be broadly categorized into two approaches: unstructured pruning, which removes individual weights based on their magnitudes or importance (Liao et al., 2023), and structured pruning, which discards entire coupled structures (Cheng et al., 2024). Although unstructured pruning is conceptually simple, it rarely yields practical acceleration on modern GPUs (e.g., Nvidia GPUs typically require over 90% sparsity for speedup (Shi et al., 2020; Wang, 2020)), while LLMs usually collapse once sparsity exceeds 50% (Song et al., 2024b). Therefore, we focus on structured pruning, which is both hardware-friendly and effective. Structured pruning can be further categorized into width pruning, which reduces hidden dimensions, and depth pruning, which removes redundant layers either statically (the same set of layers is pruned for all inputs) or dynamically (the pruned layers vary depending on the input). 3 Experimental setup

Model

For LLM-instruct, we adopt the open-source model Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT (Lambert et al., 2024), which provides publicly available weights, instruction-tuning data, and detailed training configurations. For LLM-think, we fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the OpenThoughts dataset (Guha et al., 2025), which provides diverse, high-quality reasoning examples that elicit multi-step chains of thought. 11 1 Fine-tuning was performed using Llama-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) on 8×8\times,H20 (96,GB) GPUs for 3 epochs (≈\approx,488 GPU hours). See Table 4 for details.

Both models share the same Llama-3.1-8B backbone, ensuring a controlled comparison of pruning effects. Crucially, the training datasets for both models are accessible and used during pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery. This ensures that performance recovery is conducted under the native training distribution rather than on downstream task data, providing a consistent and controlled evaluation of pruning strategies.

Evaluation Benchmarks

To systematically evaluate the instruction-following capabilities of the LLM-instruct and the reasoning capabilities of the LLM-think, we use a diverse suite of 17 tasks that can be broadly divided into instruction-following and reasoning benchmarks. For evaluation, each model is assessed on benchmarks aligned with its primary capabilities: LLM-instruct are evaluated on instruction-following benchmarks, whereas LLM-think are evaluated on reasoning benchmarks.

  • •

    Instruction Following Benchmarks To comprehensively assess pruned LLM-instruct on instruction following, we include both classification and generation tasks. For classification tasks, following (Touvron et al., 2023), we include BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), ARC-Easy / Challenge (ARC-E / C) (Clark et al., 2019), and OpenBookQA (OPQA) (Mihaylov et al., 2018). For generation tasks, we adopt a similar setup to (Lambert et al., 2024), but exclude tasks that rely heavily on explicit CoT reasoning (evaluated separately under reasoning benchmarks). Specifically, we include IFEval (IFE) (Zhou et al., 2023) to measure instruction-execution precision; TruthfulQA (TQA) (Lin et al., 2021) and PopQA (PQA) (Mallen et al., 2022) to assess factual accuracy and truthfulness; and HumanEval (HE) (Chen et al., 2021) together with HumanEval+ (HE+) (Liu et al., 2023) as constrained code-generation tasks, where strict adherence to problem specifications is critical.

  • •

    Reasoning Benchmarks To rigorously evaluate the reasoning abilities of the pruned LLM-think model, we employ five challenging benchmarks spanning mathematical, coding, and scientific domains. Specifically, AIME 2024 (AIME) and MATH-500 (MATH) (Lightman et al., 2023) assess advanced mathematical reasoning and multi-step derivation; LiveCodeBench (LCB) (Jain et al., 2024) evaluates code generation, debugging, and comprehension in complex programming tasks; and GPQA-Diamond (GPQA) (Rein et al., 2024) together with JEEBench (JEE) (Arora et al., 2023) assess nuanced scientific reasoning and the application of domain-specific knowledge.

Evaluated Pruning Methods

To systematically evaluate pruning in both LLM-instruct and LLM-think models, we consider representative methods from three main categories of structured pruning.

  • •

    Static depth pruning reduces model depth by removing entire transformer layers. We consider SLEB, an iterative method that recomputes layer-importance scores after each pruning step; ShortGPT (Men et al., 2024), which prunes layers based on input–output representation cosine similarity; and Shortened-PPL / Shortened-Taylor (Kim et al., 2024), which identify and remove layers using perplexity (PPL) and Taylor-based criteria, respectively.

  • •

    Static width pruning reduces model width by pruning attention heads or shrinking the hidden-state dimension. We adopt LLM-Pruner (Ma et al., 2023), a gradient-based method that prunes coupled structures, and SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024), which removes low-variance components from weight matrices via principal component analysis.

  • •

    Dynamic depth pruning reduces per-input computation by adaptively skipping layers or submodules. MOD (Raposo et al., 2024b) selects a subset of tokens to process in each layer via Top-kk routing. D-LLM (Jiang et al., 2024) uses a router to decide whether to execute each transformer layer. SkipGPT (Zhao et al., 2025) combines global token-aware routing with decoupled pruning of MLP and self-attention modules, and defines the pruning ratio as the mean token-level skipping rate across the two modules.

4 Effects of Calibration/Recovery Data

Before analyzing the effects of different pruning strategies, we first examine a fundamental yet often overlooked design choice in the pruning pipeline: the datasets used for calibration and post-pruning recovery. In modern LLM pruning methods, these two stages constitute the most critical components of the pipeline. Calibration estimates the importance of model structures (e.g., layers or channels) to guide pruning decisions, while post-pruning recovery aims to restore performance by adapting the remaining parameters after pruning. While prior work adopts heterogeneous datasets, their choice for calibration and recovery data is rather arbitrary.

To establish a well-founded experimental setting for subsequent analysis, we first investigate whether aligning both pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery with the model’s original training distribution is beneficial for preserving pre-pruning performance. To this end, we examine two representative pruning methods: ShortGPT for static depth pruning and SliceGPT for static width pruning. We compare general-domain corpora (e.g., C4, PTB, and WikiText2) and standard instruction-tuning datasets (e.g., Alpaca) against the model’s original training corpora, namely tulu-3-sft-mixture for LLM-instruct and openthoughts for LLM-think, under a fixed pruning ratio of 20%. Additional results that separately disentangle the effects of the calibration dataset and the post-pruning recovery dataset are reported in Appendix D.

For evaluation, we assess LLM-instruct models on IFEval, HumanEval+, and classification tasks, and evaluate LLM-think models on GSM8K using CoT prompting. The results in Figure 2 consistently show that, for both LLM-instruct and LLM-think, using the original training corpus for calibration and post-pruning recovery yields the strongest performance. While general-domain and instruction-tuning datasets are sufficient to preserve basic linguistic competence, reflected by relatively stable performance on simpler benchmarks, they fail to retain more complex capabilities, resulting in near-zero performance on challenging tasks. In contrast, calibration and recovery using the original training corpus consistently preserve strong performance across all tasks.

5 Effects of Pruning

After confirming that using the original training corpus for both pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery more effectively recovers the performance of pruned models, we adopt this configuration as our default setting in the remainder of the paper. Specifically, we fix the calibration and recovery data to match the original training distribution, thereby controlling for dataset choice and isolating the effects of different pruning strategies in subsequent analyses.

Within static depth pruning methods,

we study four representative strategies: SLEB, ShortGPT, Shortened-PPL, and Shortened-Taylor. as shown in Table 1 and Table 3, for LLM-instruct, Shortened-Taylor consistently outperforms competing methods under both 20% and 40% pruning ratios. This advantage is particularly pronounced on generation tasks, where the average performance decline remains below 7.04% at a 20% pruning ratio. Shortened-Taylor is particularly effective at identifying redundant layers for LLM-instruct. Its advantage comes from using a second-order Taylor approximation to estimate each layer’s contribution to the training loss, yielding a more sensitivity-aware notion of importance than purely local heuristics. By comparison, ShortGPT relies on input–output representation similarity, while Shortened-PPL ranks layers by the perplexity change induced by removing each layer. SLEB further introduces an iterative procedure that recomputes layer importance after every pruning step. For LLM-think, however, a markedly different regime emerges. As shown in Table 3, the performance decline of all methods exceeds 42% even at a 20% pruning ratio, indicating that removing only a small number of layers (e.g., six) leads to substantial degradation. These results suggest that static depth pruning may not be an ideal pruning strategy for LLM-think.

Within static width pruning methods,

we compare two representative strategies: LLM-Pruner and SliceGPT. As shown in Figure 4, SliceGPT consistently outperforms LLM-Pruner across all pruning ratios on both LLM-instruct and LLM-think. Table 3 shows that, on classification tasks, SliceGPT maintains a modest yet stable advantage, with the performance gap remaining small and largely insensitive to higher pruning ratios. In contrast, on generation and reasoning tasks, the gap widens substantially as pruning becomes more aggressive. One plausible explanation is the difference in their width-reduction mechanisms. SliceGPT performs subspace-based compression by estimating a low-dimensional subspace from calibration activations and removing low-variance directions, thereby shrinking hidden dimensions in a globally consistent manner. In contrast, LLM-Pruner removes structured modules (e.g., attention- or MLP-related groups) based on importance scores, potentially discarding discrete functional components that are harder to preserve under high sparsity. Overall, these results suggest that subspace-based width reduction (SliceGPT) preserves model performance more reliably than structured component deletion (LLM-Pruner) across both LLM-instruct and LLM-think.

Within dynamic depth pruning methods,

we compare three representative strategies: MOD, D-LLM, and SkipGPT. As shown in Table 3, for LLM-instruct, SkipGPT consistently and substantially outperforms both D-LLM and MOD in performance retention across all pruning ratios. This advantage becomes more pronounced on generation tasks under higher pruning ratios; even at a 60% pruning ratio, SkipGPT maintains an average performance decline below 4% across both task types, achieving near-lossless compression. For LLM-think, however, a markedly different trend emerges. Even at a 20% pruning ratio, D-LLM and SkipGPT suffer severe semantic degradation, producing repetitive and incoherent outputs, whereas only MOD retains approximately 40% of the dense model’s performance. This discrepancy raises an important question: why does SkipGPT, which achieves near-lossless performance on LLM-instruct, fail to generalize to LLM-think, while MOD preserves a non-trivial fraction of the model’s reasoning capability? As shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5, SkipGPT exhibits contrasting optimization behavior across settings. On LLM-instruct, its LoRA fine-tuning stage converges to the lowest training loss among dynamic methods. On LLM-think, however, SkipGPT’s router-tuning stage converges to a substantially higher loss than MOD. We hypothesize that this behavior may arise from SkipGPT’s highly flexible compute allocation: frequent token-wise routing changes can destabilize depth-wise computation trajectories, reducing path continuity across layers. In contrast, MOD enforces a Top-kk constrained routing policy that trades adaptivity for more consistent layer-wise structure. This fixed compute budget yields more stable optimization under predictable resource constraints, allowing MOD to preserve a substantial fraction of the model’s reasoning capability. Overall, these results suggest that SkipGPT’s highly flexible token-wise routing works well for LLM-instruct but is less reliable for LLM-think, whereas MOD’s Top-kk constraint trades adaptivity for more stable reasoning retention.

Static depth vs. width pruning.

For LLM-instruct, as shown in Table 3 and Figure 4, static depth pruning slightly outperforms width pruning on classification tasks, whereas width pruning demonstrates greater robustness on generation tasks. While both approaches perform similarly at a 20% pruning ratio, increasing the ratio to 40% leads to a markedly larger performance drop for depth pruning (55.57%) than for width pruning (41.83%). This pattern extends to LLM-think: despite marginally stronger performance from depth pruning at 20%, both methods deteriorate rapidly at higher pruning levels. At a 40% pruning ratio, depth pruning drops by 85.38%, compared to 77.69% for width pruning. This gap reflects a fundamental structural difference between depth and width pruning. While depth pruning reduces the model’s depth, width pruning primarily limits representational capacity. As a result, width pruning exhibits more stable performance on generation and reasoning tasks at higher sparsity levels. Overall, these results suggest that preserving model depth is more critical than preserving width, implying that depth should be pruned conservatively while width admits more aggressive compression.

Static vs. Dynamic Pruning.

As shown in Figure 4, on LLM-instruct, dynamic pruning methods consistently outperform static ones. In particular, both SkipGPT and MOD achieve superior performance across pruning ratios, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at higher pruning ratios. In contrast, this trend reverses on LLM-think: dynamic pruning methods consistently underperform static pruning methods. As shown in Figure 5, under a 20% pruning ratio, static pruning methods reliably converge to low-loss regions, whereas many dynamic methods display unstable or even pathological optimization dynamics and settle at substantially higher training loss. This optimization gap provides a mechanistic explanation for the weaker downstream performance of dynamic pruning on LLM-think. Notably, MOD is a clear exception among dynamic approaches, exhibiting strong and stable convergence that is comparable to static pruning methods. These results indicate that reasoning performance hinges less on whether pruning is static or dynamic than on whether the pruning strategy preserves continuous computation paths along the depth dimension. Accordingly, static width pruning methods (e.g., LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT) and dynamic pruning(MOD) perform better on LLM-think.

6 Conclusion

We study whether pruning methods developed for LLM-instruct generalize to LLM-think, where models explicitly generate long intermediate reasoning traces. Using a controlled pipeline that aligns calibration and post-pruning recovery with each model’s original training distribution, we construct matched model–dataset pairs for both paradigms and evaluate static depth pruning, static width pruning, and dynamic pruning across 17 classification, generation, and reasoning tasks. The results show clear paradigm and task-dependent trade-offs: static depth pruning is more effective for classification, whereas static width pruning degrades more gracefully for generation and reasoning. Dynamic pruning benefits classification and generation but is substantially harder to optimize for long-chain reasoning, making aggressive compute skipping risky for reasoning-intensive workloads. Overall, dynamic methods lead on classification and generation, while static pruning better preserves reasoning performance, highlighting an important gap in current dynamic pruning for LLM-think.

Limitations

Our experiments are conducted on Llama-8B–scale language models, and we do not explicitly evaluate how the observed pruning behaviors generalize across model scales. While our findings reveal clear and consistent trends within this setting, extending the analysis to smaller and larger models remains an important direction for future work.

Appendix B Related Work

The multi-layer Transformer architecture of LLMs inherently contains substantial parameter redundancy. Model pruning is a key technique to mitigate this redundancy by removing non-essential components. In practice, hardware-friendly structured pruning, which eliminates entire components such as layers, channels, or attention heads, has become the dominant approach and can be broadly categorized into static depth, static width, and dynamic depth methods.

B.1 Static Depth Pruning

Static depth pruning reduces model depth by removing fixed Transformer layers or their internal submodules (Attention or MLP). The main challenge is to reliably estimate layer importance. Most existing approaches rely on one-shot scoring. Shortened Llama (Kim et al., 2024) introduces three types of importance estimators: Magnitude, which approximates a layer’s contribution using weight norms; Taylor, which estimates the change in loss when the layer’s weights are removed; and PPL, which directly measures the increase in PPL after removing a layer. These methods often underestimate the importance of early and late layers, so practical pruning pipelines typically keep the first four and the last two layers intact. ShortGPT (Men et al., 2024) further proposes Block Influence (BI), which measures redundancy by comparing the cosine similarity between a layer’s input and output. In contrast, SLEB (Song et al., 2024a) adopts an iterative strategy, recomputing importance scores after each pruning step for the remaining layers.

While these approaches focus primarily on layer-level redundancy, they overlook finer-grained intra-layer structure. To address this, Joint Layer Drop (He et al., 2024) removes Attention and MLP modules jointly based on their similarity, and BlockPruner (Zhong et al., 2025) decomposes each layer into Attention and MLP blocks for iterative pruning. Beyond direct deletion, Laco (Yang et al., 2024b) introduces layer collapse, replacing the parameters of multiple layers with a single layer while preserving the internal structure of the LLM.

B.2 Static Width Pruning

Static width pruning aims to reduce the computational cost of Transformer models by removing redundant components within submodules, such as attention heads or MLP neurons, while typically preserving the residual stream dimensionality. A central challenge lies in defining reliable importance criteria for identifying removable components.

Based on how pruning decisions vary across layers, existing approaches can be broadly categorized as uniform or non-uniform in the pruning process. Non-uniform methods, such as Sheared-LLaMA (Xia et al., 2023), LLM-Pruner (Ma et al., 2023), and FLAP (An et al., 2024), leverage importance metrics, such as weight norms, Taylor-based sensitivity, or activation statistics, to adaptively determine pruning decisions for each layer or submodule. Although these methods typically retain a consistent post-pruning layer structure, they primarily reduce submodule-internal widths rather than the residual stream, which limits their ability to achieve substantial hardware-level acceleration with standard inference kernels.

In contrast, approaches such as SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024) directly compress the residual stream by projecting hidden representations onto a lower-dimensional subspace shared across all layers. This uniform reduction of the residual stream dimension yields consistent tensor shapes throughout the network, enabling efficient utilization of optimized GPU kernels and resulting in more stable inference and tangible speedups.

B.3 Dynamic Depth Pruning

Unlike static methods, dynamic pruning customizes the computational path for each input at inference time, reducing computation by executing only the essential components.

A widely studied approach is early exit (Schuster et al., 2022; Varshney et al., 2023; Del Corro et al., 2023; Din et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024). By inserting intermediate classifiers at multiple depths, early exit allows “simple” inputs to terminate inference early, bypassing the remaining layers. While this can substantially accelerate inference, it may compromise the model’s ability for deep semantic reasoning.

Another paradigm is layer skipping, where router modules dynamically determine whether a layer should be executed or bypassed. Layer skipping can be divided into vertical dynamics (D-LLM, SkipGPT) and horizontal dynamics (MOD). Vertical dynamics control the allocation of computation along the model depth based on token importance, whereas horizontal dynamics distribute computation unevenly across the sequence dimension using a Top-kk constraint. For vertical dynamics, D-LLM (Jiang et al., 2024) introduces a dynamic decision module at each layer to adaptively execute network units and implements an efficient eviction strategy for the KV cache. Similarly, SkipGPT (Zhao et al., 2025) combines global token-aware routing with decoupled pruning of MLP and self-attention layers, enabling fine-grained resource allocation. For horizontal dynamics, MOD (Raposo et al., 2024b) applies Top-kk routing to select which tokens are processed by each layer’s self-attention and MLP modules. Together, these methods provide a flexible framework for balancing inference efficiency and per-input model performance.

Appendix C Experiments Details

For LLM-instruct, all experiments are conducted on a single A800 GPU without using DeepSpeed. We adopt Llama 3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT, obtained through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Llama 3.1-8B (Lambert et al., 2024), as our dense baseline model. The SFT training corpus is adopted both as the calibration set for model pruning and as the training set for subsequent LoRA fine-tuning. Specifically, we reserve approximately 0.1% of the corpus as the test set and use the remainder for training. We train all baselines for 10,000 steps with batch size 16, a cosine learning-rate schedule, and a warmup ratio of 0.1, and we select the learning rate via grid search for each baseline. The maximum sequence length is 4,096 tokens.

For the LLM-think, no reasoning-oriented model exists with fully open-source training data. To address this gap, we fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the OpenThoughts dataset, resulting in a new model, Llama-3.1-3-8B-Instruct-OpenThoughts. The detailed hyperparameters are summarized in Table 4. For all baseline pruning methods, experiments are conducted on a single A800 GPU with DeepSpeed Stage-2 offloading and gradient checkpointing enabled. Following the setup in LLM-instruct experiments, the OpenThoughts dataset is used both as the calibration set for model pruning and as the training set for subsequent LoRA fine-tuning. Specifically, we adopt a batch size of 16 and train all baselines for 3,000 steps, applying early stopping if the training converges before reaching this limit. For each baseline, we conduct a grid search over learning rates to select the optimal value. We employ a cosine decay learning rate schedule and set the warmup ratio to 0.1.

Appendix D Additional Empirical Findings on Calibration and Post-training Datasets

In this section, we provide additional observations on calibration and post-pruning recovery datasets.

The Impact of Calibration Set Size

Our results reveal a strong dependence on calibration-set size. When using tulu-3-sft-mixture, Table 5 shows that SliceGPT’s performance increases sharply as the number of calibration examples grows from 128 to 512, but plateaus beyond 1024 examples, forming a clear saturation trend. This behavior suggests that the model rapidly extracts most of the usable calibration signal from relatively small sample sizes.

The Impact of Calibration Datasets.

In this subsection, we isolate the effect of calibration datasets. As shown in Figure 6 and Table 6, SliceGPT is highly sensitive to the choice of calibration data, whereas ShortGPT exhibits substantially more stable behavior.

The Impact of Post-training Datasets.

In this subsection, we isolate the effect of post-pruning recovery datasets. As shown in Figure 7 and Table 7, our experimental results indicate that, for both LLM-instruct and LLM-think, post-training recovery is most effective when conducted on the original training corpus. This pattern holds consistently for both SliceGPT and ShortGPT.

Appendix E Repetitive Generation in LLM-Think

In this section, we present several failure cases of dynamic depth pruning methods, namely D-LLM and SkipGPT. Even under a 20% pruning ratio, these methods exhibit severe semantic degradation, producing repetitive and incoherent outputs that persist until the maximum generation length is reached.

Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly costly to deploy, motivating extensive research on model pruning. However, most existing studies focus on instruction-following LLMs, leaving it unclear whether established pruning strategies transfer to reasoning-augmented models that explicitly generate long intermediate reasoning traces. In this work, we conduct a controlled study of pruning for both instruction-following ( LLM-instruct ) and reasoning-augmented ( LLM-think ) models. To isolate the effects of pruning, we align pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery data with each model’s original training distribution, which we show yield more stable and reliable pruning behavior. We evaluate static depth pruning, static width pruning, and dynamic pruning across 17 tasks spanning classification, generation, and reasoning. Our results reveal clear paradigm-dependent differences: depth pruning outperforms width pruning on classification tasks, while width pruning is more robust for generation and reasoning. Moreover, static pruning better preserves reasoning performance, whereas dynamic pruning excels on classification and generation but remains challenging for long-chain reasoning. These findings underscore the need for pruning strategies that explicitly account for the distinct characteristics of reasoning-augmented LLMs. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LRM-Pruning .
1 Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) have led to significant advances in natural language processing and enabled impactful applications across a wide range of domains Zhu et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2024) ; Pang et al. (2024) ; Abbasian et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Guan et al. (2025) . However, their strong empirical performance comes with substantial computational costs, posing major challenges for practical use in resource-constrained environments ( Zhong et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) .

Static depth pruning removes entire layers, static width pruning reduces hidden dimensions (neurons or attention heads), and dynamic depth pruning adaptively skips layers, attention blocks, or MLP modules depending on the input.
Model pruning has emerged as one of the most widely adopted approaches for improving LLM efficiency Sun et al. (2024) ; Ma et al. (2023) ; Men et al. (2024) . Early work has primarily focused on static pruning , where a fixed subset of parameters is removed prior to deployment. Within this paradigm, static depth pruning reduces inference cost by removing entire layers, shortening the model and decreasing sequential computation ( Men et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, static width pruning reduces per-layer computation by shrinking hidden dimensions or pruning channels while preserving the original network depth ( Ma et al., 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) . More recently, dynamic pruning has been explored, which adaptively skips parts of the computation during inference based on input-dependent signals, rather than permanently removing parameters ( Raposo et al., 2024a ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Together, these techniques form a mature toolkit for accelerating LLMs.
Meanwhile, the LLM landscape is undergoing a paradigm shift from instruction-following models, which we refer to as LLM-instruct , to reasoning-augmented models, denoted as LLM-think Xu et al. (2025) ; DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025) . Unlike LLM-instruct ( Yang et al., 2024a ) , which generate a direct response with reasoning implicitly embedded, LLM-think explicitly externalize their reasoning process by producing step-by-step intermediate traces prior to the final answer ( Wei et al., 2022 ) . While this shift substantially improves performance on complex tasks, it also results in markedly longer generations, often spanning thousands of tokens ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025a ) . Despite these fundamental changes in model behavior and output characteristics, existing pruning research has almost exclusively focused on LLM-instruct. This gap motivates a central question: does pruning for LLM-think require new strategies, or can existing approaches generalize across paradigms?
Addressing this question necessitates a carefully controlled pruning pipeline. We therefore begin by revisiting a critical yet often overlooked design choice in prior work: the selection of datasets used for pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery . However, prior studies adopt highly heterogeneous datasets for these stages, ranging from general-domain corpora to instruction-tuning data, often without systematic justification ( Raffel et al., 2020 ; Taori et al., 2023 ) . Such inconsistency introduces confounding factors, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of pruning from those of distribution mismatch.
To enable a principled comparison, we adopt a controlled setting in which calibration and recovery data are strictly aligned with the original training distribution of the target model. Under this setting, we construct matched model–dataset pairs for both paradigms. For LLM-instruct , we use the open-sourced Tulu model ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) together with its full instruction-following fine-tuning corpus. For LLM-think , we derive a reasoning-augmented counterpart by further fine-tuning the same base model on OpenThoughts ( Guha et al., 2025 ) , a dataset designed to elicit explicit multi-step reasoning across diverse difficulty levels. This alignment ensures that each model is pruned, calibrated, and recovered using data drawn from its own training distribution, thereby isolating the impact of pruning itself.
As we show empirically, such alignment best preserves pre-pruning performance and leads to substantially more stable and effective pruning behavior compared to using mismatched datasets.
Under this controlled setting, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three categories of pruning strategies on both LLM-instruct and LLM-think across 17 diverse classification, generation, and reasoning tasks. Our experiments yield several key empirical findings. First, static depth pruning is more effective than static width pruning on classification tasks, whereas the opposite trend holds for generation and reasoning tasks, where width pruning degrades performance more gracefully. Second, dynamic pruning with unconstrained token-level routing benefits classification and generation but proves substantially harder to optimize for long-chain reasoning, suggesting that aggressive computation skipping is particularly risky for reasoning-intensive workloads. Finally, while dynamic pruning generally outperforms static methods on classification and generation, static pruning retains higher performance on reasoning tasks, highlighting an important gap in current dynamic pruning approaches.
2 Background
LLM-instruct and LLM-thinking
The rapid progress of LLMs has not only improved their instruction-following ability but also expanded their scope toward explicit reasoning. This shift has given rise to two major families: instruction-following models ( LLM-instruct ), which are optimized to produce outputs that closely align with user-specified instructions, and reasoning-augmented models ( LLM-think ), which are trained to generate long chains of thought (CoT) reasoning before arriving at final answers.
Although the two are built upon the same underlying architecture, recent studies show that they diverge significantly in both internal representations and emergent behaviors.
Mechanistically, LLM-think retain richer contextual information across layers and exhibit higher token-level entropy ( Skean et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . In terms of attention, LLM-instruct generally display diverse specialization across heads, with each attending to different token subsets ( Fu et al., 2024 ) , whereas LLM-think show considerable overlap in tokens attended by different heads ( Yang et al., 2025b ) .
Formalizing Structure Pruning Strategies
Model pruning in LLMs can be broadly categorized into two approaches: unstructured pruning , which removes individual weights based on their magnitudes or importance ( Liao et al., 2023 ) , and structured pruning , which discards entire coupled structures ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) . Although unstructured pruning is conceptually simple, it rarely yields practical acceleration on modern GPUs (e.g., Nvidia GPUs typically require over 90% sparsity for speedup ( Shi et al., 2020 ; Wang, 2020 ) ), while LLMs usually collapse once sparsity exceeds 50% ( Song et al., 2024b ) . Therefore, we focus on structured pruning, which is both hardware-friendly and effective. Structured pruning can be further categorized into width pruning , which reduces hidden dimensions, and depth pruning , which removes redundant layers either statically (the same set of layers is pruned for all inputs) or dynamically (the pruned layers vary depending on the input). 3 Experimental setup
Model
For LLM-instruct, we adopt the open-source model Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , which provides publicly available weights, instruction-tuning data, and detailed training configurations. For LLM-think, we fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the OpenThoughts dataset ( Guha et al., 2025 ) , which provides diverse, high-quality reasoning examples that elicit multi-step chains of thought. 1 1

Fine-tuning was performed using Llama-Factory ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) on 8 × 8\times ,H20 (96,GB) GPUs for 3 epochs ( ≈ \approx ,488 GPU hours). See Table 4 for details.
Both models share the same Llama-3.1-8B backbone, ensuring a controlled comparison of pruning effects. Crucially, the training datasets for both models are accessible and used during pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery. This ensures that performance recovery is conducted under the native training distribution rather than on downstream task data, providing a consistent and controlled evaluation of pruning strategies.
Evaluation Benchmarks
To systematically evaluate the instruction-following capabilities of the LLM-instruct and the reasoning capabilities of the LLM-think, we use a diverse suite of 17 tasks that can be broadly divided into instruction-following and reasoning benchmarks.
For evaluation, each model is assessed on benchmarks aligned with its primary capabilities: LLM-instruct are evaluated on instruction-following benchmarks, whereas LLM-think are evaluated on reasoning benchmarks.

Instruction Following Benchmarks
To comprehensively assess pruned LLM-instruct on instruction following, we include both classification and generation tasks. For classification tasks, following ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) , we include BoolQ ( Clark et al., 2019 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , WinoGrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ) , ARC-Easy / Challenge (ARC-E / C) ( Clark et al., 2019 ) , and OpenBookQA (OPQA) ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) . For generation tasks, we adopt a similar setup to ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , but exclude tasks that rely heavily on explicit CoT reasoning (evaluated separately under reasoning benchmarks). Specifically, we include IFEval (IFE) ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) to measure instruction-execution precision; TruthfulQA (TQA) ( Lin et al., 2021 ) and PopQA (PQA) ( Mallen et al., 2022 ) to assess factual accuracy and truthfulness; and HumanEval (HE) ( Chen et al., 2021 ) together with HumanEval+ (HE+) ( Liu et al., 2023 ) as constrained code-generation tasks, where strict adherence to problem specifications is critical.
•
Reasoning Benchmarks To rigorously evaluate the reasoning abilities of the pruned LLM-think model, we employ five challenging benchmarks spanning mathematical, coding, and scientific domains. Specifically, AIME 2024 (AIME) and MATH-500 (MATH) ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) assess advanced mathematical reasoning and multi-step derivation; LiveCodeBench (LCB) ( Jain et al., 2024 ) evaluates code generation, debugging, and comprehension in complex programming tasks; and GPQA-Diamond (GPQA) ( Rein et al., 2024 ) together with JEEBench (JEE) ( Arora et al., 2023 ) assess nuanced scientific reasoning and the application of domain-specific knowledge.
Evaluated Pruning Methods
To systematically evaluate pruning in both LLM-instruct and LLM-think models, we consider representative methods from three main categories of structured pruning.
•
Static depth pruning reduces model depth by removing entire transformer layers. We consider SLEB, an iterative method that recomputes layer-importance scores after each pruning step; ShortGPT ( Men et al., 2024 ) , which prunes layers based on input–output representation cosine similarity; and Shortened-PPL / Shortened-Taylor ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , which identify and remove layers using perplexity (PPL) and Taylor-based criteria, respectively.
•
Static width pruning reduces model width by pruning attention heads or shrinking the hidden-state dimension. We adopt LLM-Pruner ( Ma et al., 2023 ) , a gradient-based method that prunes coupled structures, and SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , which removes low-variance components from weight matrices via principal component analysis.
•
Dynamic depth pruning reduces per-input computation by adaptively skipping layers or submodules. MOD ( Raposo et al., 2024b ) selects a subset of tokens to process in each layer via Top- k k routing. D-LLM ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) uses a router to decide whether to execute each transformer layer. SkipGPT ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) combines global token-aware routing with decoupled pruning of MLP and self-attention modules, and defines the pruning ratio as the mean token-level skipping rate across the two modules.
4 Effects of Calibration/Recovery Data
Before analyzing the effects of different pruning strategies, we first examine a fundamental yet often overlooked design choice in the pruning pipeline: the datasets used for calibration and post-pruning recovery . In modern LLM pruning methods, these two stages constitute the most critical components of the pipeline. Calibration estimates the importance of model structures (e.g., layers or channels) to guide pruning decisions, while post-pruning recovery aims to restore performance by adapting the remaining parameters after pruning. While prior work adopts heterogeneous datasets, their choice for calibration and recovery data is rather arbitrary.
To establish a well-founded experimental setting for subsequent analysis, we first investigate whether aligning both pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery with the model’s original training distribution is beneficial for preserving pre-pruning performance. To this end, we examine two representative pruning methods: ShortGPT for static depth pruning and SliceGPT for static width pruning. We compare general-domain corpora (e.g., C4, PTB, and WikiText2) and standard instruction-tuning datasets (e.g., Alpaca) against the model’s original training corpora, namely tulu-3-sft-mixture for LLM-instruct and openthoughts for LLM-think, under a fixed pruning ratio of 20%. Additional results that separately disentangle the effects of the calibration dataset and the post-pruning recovery dataset are reported in Appendix D .

For evaluation, we assess LLM-instruct models on IFEval, HumanEval+, and classification tasks, and evaluate LLM-think models on GSM8K using CoT prompting. The results in Figure 2 consistently show that, for both LLM-instruct and LLM-think, using the original training corpus for calibration and post-pruning recovery yields the strongest performance. While general-domain and instruction-tuning datasets are sufficient to preserve basic linguistic competence, reflected by relatively stable performance on simpler benchmarks, they fail to retain more complex capabilities, resulting in near-zero performance on challenging tasks. In contrast, calibration and recovery using the original training corpus consistently preserve strong performance across all tasks.
For both LLM-instruct and LLM-think, aligning pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery with the model’s original training corpus consistently yields superior preservation of pre-pruning capabilities.
Conclusion
5 Effects of Pruning
After confirming that using the original training corpus for both pruning calibration and post-pruning recovery more effectively recovers the performance of pruned models, we adopt this configuration as our default setting in the remainder of the paper. Specifically, we fix the calibration and recovery data to match the original training distribution, thereby controlling for dataset choice and isolating the effects of different pruning strategies in subsequent analyses.

Within static depth pruning methods,
we study four representative strategies: SLEB , ShortGPT , Shortened-PPL , and Shortened-Taylor . as shown in Table 1 and Table 3 , for LLM-instruct, Shortened-Taylor consistently outperforms competing methods under both 20% and 40% pruning ratios. This advantage is particularly pronounced on generation tasks, where the average performance decline remains below 7.04% at a 20% pruning ratio.
Shortened-Taylor is particularly effective at identifying redundant layers for LLM-instruct. Its advantage comes from using a second-order Taylor approximation to estimate each layer’s contribution to the training loss, yielding a more sensitivity-aware notion of importance than purely local heuristics. By comparison, ShortGPT relies on input–output representation similarity, while Shortened-PPL ranks layers by the perplexity change induced by removing each layer. SLEB further introduces an iterative procedure that recomputes layer importance after every pruning step.
For LLM-think, however, a markedly different regime emerges. As shown in Table 3 , the performance decline of all methods exceeds 42% even at a 20% pruning ratio, indicating that removing only a small number of layers (e.g., six) leads to substantial degradation. These results suggest that static depth pruning may not be an ideal pruning strategy for LLM-think.

Within static width pruning methods,
we compare two representative strategies: LLM-Pruner and SliceGPT .
As shown in Figure 4 , SliceGPT consistently outperforms LLM-Pruner across all pruning ratios on both LLM-instruct and LLM-think. Table 3 shows that, on classification tasks, SliceGPT maintains a modest yet stable advantage, with the performance gap remaining small and largely insensitive to higher pruning ratios. In contrast, on generation and reasoning tasks, the gap widens substantially as pruning becomes more aggressive.
One plausible explanation is the difference in their width-reduction mechanisms. SliceGPT performs subspace-based compression by estimating a low-dimensional subspace from calibration activations and removing low-variance directions, thereby shrinking hidden dimensions in a globally consistent manner. In contrast, LLM-Pruner removes structured modules (e.g., attention- or MLP-related groups) based on importance scores, potentially discarding discrete functional components that are harder to preserve under high sparsity. Overall, these results suggest that subspace-based width reduction (SliceGPT) preserves model performance more reliably than structured component deletion (LLM-Pruner) across both LLM-instruct and LLM-think.

Within dynamic depth pruning methods,
we compare three representative strategies: MOD, D-LLM, and SkipGPT. As shown in Table 3 , for LLM-instruct, SkipGPT consistently and substantially outperforms both D-LLM and MOD in performance retention across all pruning ratios. This advantage becomes more pronounced on generation tasks under higher pruning ratios; even at a 60% pruning ratio, SkipGPT maintains an average performance decline below 4% across both task types, achieving near-lossless compression.
For LLM-think, however, a markedly different trend emerges. Even at a 20% pruning ratio, D-LLM and SkipGPT suffer severe semantic degradation, producing repetitive and incoherent outputs, whereas only MOD retains approximately 40% of the dense model’s performance. This discrepancy raises an important question: why does SkipGPT, which achieves near-lossless performance on LLM-instruct, fail to generalize to LLM-think, while MOD preserves a non-trivial fraction of the model’s reasoning capability?
As shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5 , SkipGPT exhibits contrasting optimization behavior across settings. On LLM-instruct, its LoRA fine-tuning stage converges to the lowest training loss among dynamic methods. On LLM-think, however, SkipGPT’s router-tuning stage converges to a substantially higher loss than MOD.
We hypothesize that this behavior may arise from SkipGPT’s highly flexible compute allocation: frequent token-wise routing changes can destabilize depth-wise computation trajectories, reducing path continuity across layers. In contrast, MOD enforces a Top- k k constrained routing policy that trades adaptivity for more consistent layer-wise structure. This fixed compute budget yields more stable optimization under predictable resource constraints, allowing MOD to preserve a substantial fraction of the model’s reasoning capability.
Overall, these results suggest that SkipGPT’s highly flexible token-wise routing works well for LLM-instruct but is less reliable for LLM-think, whereas MOD’s Top- k k constraint trades adaptivity for more stable reasoning retention.

Static depth vs. width pruning.
For LLM-instruct, as shown in Table 3 and Figure 4 , static depth pruning slightly outperforms width pruning on classification tasks, whereas width pruning demonstrates greater robustness on generation tasks. While both approaches perform similarly at a 20% pruning ratio, increasing the ratio to 40% leads to a markedly larger performance drop for depth pruning (55.57%) than for width pruning (41.83%).
This pattern extends to LLM-think: despite marginally stronger performance from depth pruning at 20%, both methods deteriorate rapidly at higher pruning levels. At a 40% pruning ratio, depth pruning drops by 85.38%, compared to 77.69% for width pruning.
This gap reflects a fundamental structural difference between depth and width pruning. While depth pruning reduces the model’s depth, width pruning primarily limits representational capacity. As a result, width pruning exhibits more stable performance on generation and reasoning tasks at higher sparsity levels.
Overall, these results suggest that preserving model depth is more critical than preserving width, implying that depth should be pruned conservatively while width admits more aggressive compression.
At higher sparsity levels, preserving model depth is more critical than preserving width.
Conclusion
Static vs. Dynamic Pruning.
As shown in Figure 4 , on LLM-instruct, dynamic pruning methods consistently outperform static ones. In particular, both SkipGPT and MOD achieve superior performance across pruning ratios, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at higher pruning ratios.
In contrast, this trend reverses on LLM-think: dynamic pruning methods consistently underperform static pruning methods. As shown in Figure 5 , under a 20% pruning ratio, static pruning methods reliably converge to low-loss regions, whereas many dynamic methods display unstable or even pathological optimization dynamics and settle at substantially higher training loss. This optimization gap provides a mechanistic explanation for the weaker downstream performance of dynamic pruning on LLM-think. Notably, MOD is a clear exception among dynamic approaches, exhibiting strong and stable convergence that is comparable to static pruning methods.
These results indicate that reasoning performance hinges less on whether pruning is static or dynamic than on whether the pruning strategy preserves continuous computation paths along the depth dimension. Accordingly, static width pruning methods (e.g., LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT) and dynamic pruning(MOD) perform better on LLM-think.
For LLM-instruct, dynamic pruning yields the best performance, whereas for LLM-think, static pruning retains higher performance.
Conclusion
6 Conclusion
We study whether pruning methods developed for LLM-instruct generalize to LLM-think, where models explicitly generate long intermediate reasoning traces. Using a controlled pipeline that aligns calibration and post-pruning recovery with each model’s original training distribution, we construct matched model–dataset pairs for both paradigms and evaluate static depth pruning, static width pruning, and dynamic pruning across 17 classification, generation, and reasoning tasks. The results show clear paradigm and task-dependent trade-offs: static depth pruning is more effective for classification, whereas static width pruning degrades more gracefully for generation and reasoning. Dynamic pruning benefits classification and generation but is substantially harder to optimize for long-chain reasoning, making aggressive compute skipping risky for reasoning-intensive workloads. Overall, dynamic methods lead on classification and generation, while static pruning better preserves reasoning performance, highlighting an important gap in current dynamic pruning for LLM-think.
Limitations
Our experiments are conducted on Llama-8B–scale language models, and we do not explicitly evaluate how the observed pruning behaviors generalize across model scales. While our findings reveal clear and consistent trends within this setting, extending the analysis to smaller and larger models remains an important direction for future work.

Appendix B Related Work
The multi-layer Transformer architecture of LLMs inherently contains substantial parameter redundancy. Model pruning is a key technique to mitigate this redundancy by removing non-essential components. In practice, hardware-friendly structured pruning, which eliminates entire components such as layers, channels, or attention heads, has become the dominant approach and can be broadly categorized into static depth, static width, and dynamic depth methods.
B.1 Static Depth Pruning
Static depth pruning reduces model depth by removing fixed Transformer layers or their internal submodules (Attention or MLP). The main challenge is to reliably estimate layer importance. Most existing approaches rely on one-shot scoring. Shortened Llama ( Kim et al., 2024 ) introduces three types of importance estimators: Magnitude, which approximates a layer’s contribution using weight norms; Taylor, which estimates the change in loss when the layer’s weights are removed; and PPL, which directly measures the increase in PPL after removing a layer. These methods often underestimate the importance of early and late layers, so practical pruning pipelines typically keep the first four and the last two layers intact. ShortGPT ( Men et al., 2024 ) further proposes Block Influence (BI), which measures redundancy by comparing the cosine similarity between a layer’s input and output. In contrast, SLEB ( Song et al., 2024a ) adopts an iterative strategy, recomputing importance scores after each pruning step for the remaining layers.
While these approaches focus primarily on layer-level redundancy, they overlook finer-grained intra-layer structure. To address this, Joint Layer Drop ( He et al., 2024 ) removes Attention and MLP modules jointly based on their similarity, and BlockPruner ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) decomposes each layer into Attention and MLP blocks for iterative pruning. Beyond direct deletion, Laco ( Yang et al., 2024b ) introduces layer collapse, replacing the parameters of multiple layers with a single layer while preserving the internal structure of the LLM.
B.2 Static Width Pruning
Static width pruning aims to reduce the computational cost of Transformer models by removing redundant components within submodules, such as attention heads or MLP neurons, while typically preserving the residual stream dimensionality. A central challenge lies in defining reliable importance criteria for identifying removable components.
Based on how pruning decisions vary across layers, existing approaches can be broadly categorized as uniform or non-uniform in the pruning process. Non-uniform methods, such as Sheared-LLaMA ( Xia et al., 2023 ) , LLM-Pruner ( Ma et al., 2023 ) , and FLAP ( An et al., 2024 ) , leverage importance metrics, such as weight norms, Taylor-based sensitivity, or activation statistics, to adaptively determine pruning decisions for each layer or submodule.
Although these methods typically retain a consistent post-pruning layer structure, they primarily reduce submodule-internal widths rather than the residual stream, which limits their ability to achieve substantial hardware-level acceleration with standard inference kernels.
In contrast, approaches such as SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) directly compress the residual stream by projecting hidden representations onto a lower-dimensional subspace shared across all layers. This uniform reduction of the residual stream dimension yields consistent tensor shapes throughout the network, enabling efficient utilization of optimized GPU kernels and resulting in more stable inference and tangible speedups.
B.3 Dynamic Depth Pruning
Unlike static methods, dynamic pruning customizes the computational path for each input at inference time, reducing computation by executing only the essential components.
A widely studied approach is early exit ( Schuster et al., 2022 ; Varshney et al., 2023 ; Del Corro et al., 2023 ; Din et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2024 ) . By inserting intermediate classifiers at multiple depths, early exit allows “simple” inputs to terminate inference early, bypassing the remaining layers. While this can substantially accelerate inference, it may compromise the model’s ability for deep semantic reasoning.
Another paradigm is layer skipping, where router modules dynamically determine whether a layer should be executed or bypassed. Layer skipping can be divided into vertical dynamics (D-LLM, SkipGPT) and horizontal dynamics (MOD). Vertical dynamics control the allocation of computation along the model depth based on token importance, whereas horizontal dynamics distribute computation unevenly across the sequence dimension using a Top- k k constraint.
For vertical dynamics , D-LLM ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) introduces a dynamic decision module at each layer to adaptively execute network units and implements an efficient eviction strategy for the KV cache. Similarly, SkipGPT ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) combines global token-aware routing with decoupled pruning of MLP and self-attention layers, enabling fine-grained resource allocation. For horizontal dynamics , MOD ( Raposo et al., 2024b ) applies Top- k k routing to select which tokens are processed by each layer’s self-attention and MLP modules. Together, these methods provide a flexible framework for balancing inference efficiency and per-input model performance.

Appendix C Experiments Details
For LLM-instruct, all experiments are conducted on a single A800 GPU without using DeepSpeed. We adopt Llama 3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT, obtained through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Llama 3.1-8B ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , as our dense baseline model. The SFT training corpus is adopted both as the calibration set for model pruning and as the training set for subsequent LoRA fine-tuning. Specifically, we reserve approximately 0.1% of the corpus as the test set and use the remainder for training. We train all baselines for 10,000 steps with batch size 16, a cosine learning-rate schedule, and a warmup ratio of 0.1, and we select the learning rate via grid search for each baseline. The maximum sequence length is 4,096 tokens.
For the LLM-think, no reasoning-oriented model exists with fully open-source training data. To address this gap, we fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the OpenThoughts dataset, resulting in a new model, Llama-3.1-3-8B-Instruct-OpenThoughts. The detailed hyperparameters are summarized in Table 4 . For all baseline pruning methods, experiments are conducted on a single A800 GPU with DeepSpeed Stage-2 offloading and gradient checkpointing enabled.
Following the setup in LLM-instruct experiments, the OpenThoughts dataset is used both as the calibration set for model pruning and as the training set for subsequent LoRA fine-tuning. Specifically, we adopt a batch size of 16 and train all baselines for 3,000 steps, applying early stopping if the training converges before reaching this limit. For each baseline, we conduct a grid search over learning rates to select the optimal value. We employ a cosine decay learning rate schedule and set the warmup ratio to 0.1.

Appendix D Additional Empirical Findings on Calibration and Post-training Datasets
In this section, we provide additional observations on calibration and post-pruning recovery datasets.
The Impact of Calibration Set Size
Our results reveal a strong dependence on calibration-set size. When using tulu-3-sft-mixture , Table 5 shows that SliceGPT’s performance increases sharply as the number of calibration examples grows from 128 to 512, but plateaus beyond 1024 examples, forming a clear saturation trend. This behavior suggests that the model rapidly extracts most of the usable calibration signal from relatively small sample sizes.
The Impact of Calibration Datasets.
In this subsection, we isolate the effect of calibration datasets. As shown in Figure 6 and Table 6 , SliceGPT is highly sensitive to the choice of calibration data, whereas ShortGPT exhibits substantially more stable behavior.
The Impact of Post-training Datasets.
In this subsection, we isolate the effect of post-pruning recovery datasets. As shown in Figure 7 and Table 7 , our experimental results indicate that, for both LLM-instruct and LLM-think, post-training recovery is most effective when conducted on the original training corpus. This pattern holds consistently for both SliceGPT and ShortGPT.
